Eggs of the Canada goose (Branta canadensis) are incubated for a duration of approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days] when maintained at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal condition typically provided by the attending female during the nesting period. The incubating adult carefully regulates the microclimate of the nest, ensuring consistent heat transfer to the developing embryo within the calcareous egg. Upon hatching, the precocial chick emerges with a wet weight at birth of 60 grams [Wwb = 60 grams], a relatively modest mass that belies the rapid growth phase that follows. These goslings are soon capable of independent locomotion and begin to forage alongside their parents shortly after the yolk absorption is completed. The initial mass of the gosling is a crucial determinant of early survival, as larger neonates tend to exhibit higher thermoregulatory capacity and greater resistance to starvation during the first days of life. Field studies across multiple populations have consistently recorded hatching masses clustered around this value, with minor variation attributed to maternal condition and clutch size. The brief incubation period is typical for a large-bodied waterfowl species and reflects a trade-off between developmental completeness and the need to minimize egg predation risk in open-nesting habitats.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period of this species, which is approximately 41.1 °C [T = 41.1 °C], the young goslings progress through a predictable sequence of developmental milestones. The age at fledging, defined as the time since birth at fledging when the juvenile bird achieves its first sustained flight, has been documented at approximately 52.5 days [tx = approximately 52.5 days] at a temperature of 41.1 °C [T = 41.1 °C]. This value, equivalent to roughly 7.5 weeks, marks the point at which the flight feathers have fully matured and the young individual can escape predators and join adults in aerial movements. During the pre-fledging period, the growing juvenile bird passes through a phase of rapid mass increase, adding substantial body tissue in preparation for the energetic demands of flight. Sexual maturity in male Canada geese, however, is not achieved until considerably later. Puberty, or the onset of gonadal maturation, is typically reached at around 157.5 days after hatching [tp = around 157.5 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the energy required to complete somatic at a temperature of 41.1 °C [T = 41.1 °C] growth. This delayed maturation is consistent with the life-history strategy of a long-lived, iteroparous species that prioritizes body development before committing resources to reproduction. The juvenile period is therefore characterized by intense feeding activity and gradual social integration into larger flocks.

The first brood event for a Canada goose does not coincide with the attainment of puberty, but rather occurs later once the individual has acquired sufficient experience and body condition. The time since birth at first brood for this species is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days] under the standard thermal conditions of 41.1 °C [T = 41.1 °C]. This two-year delay between reaching sexual maturity and initiating a first breeding attempt is a well-documented feature of the species' reproductive biology, reflecting the need for young adults to secure a suitable nesting territory and form a stable pair bond. Males compete intensively for high-quality nesting sites, and only those in prime condition tend to successfully initiate a clutch during their second calendar year. Females, likewise, benefit from an extended period of foraging experience that enhances their ability to lay a full complement of eggs. The maximum recorded lifespan for Canada geese in the wild is considerable, with the oldest documented individuals living for up to 42 years [am = up to 42 years] when maintained at an average body temperature of 41.1 °C [T = 41.1 °C]. This extraordinary longevity is among the highest recorded for any anseriform species and underscores the slow pace of life history in this lineage, where high adult survival compensates for modest annual reproductive output.

Female Canada geese typically produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], and the clutch size itself ranges from two to nine eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two to nine eggs per clutch]. This reproductive output places the species at the moderate end of the spectrum among large-bodied waterfowl. The adult female mass at asymptotic size is a key determinant of egg size and clutch volume. The ultimate wet weight for adult females of Branta canadensis typically reaches approximately 1313 grams [Wwi = approximately 1313 grams], though considerable geographic variation exists across the species' extensive range. Adult males, by contrast, attain a larger ultimate wet weight that averages approximately 1500 grams [Wwi = approximately 1500 grams] in many populations. This sexual size dimorphism, with males being roughly 15% heavier than females, is common among geese and is linked to the intense male-male competition for territories and mates during the breeding season. The larger body mass of males also provides a reserve of energy that supports their vigilant nest defense and aggressive exclusion of conspecifics.

Nesting success in Canada geese is closely tied to the timing of spring snowmelt and the availability of nutritious forage for the gravid female. After the eggs are laid, the incubating adult undergoes a period of fasting or near-fasting, relying on stored body reserves to maintain the consistent incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] inside the nest. Once the young have fledged, the family unit remains cohesive for several weeks as the parents continue to provide protection and guidance during the post-fledging dispersal phase. Eventually, the nutritional independence onset occurs as the juvenile birds begin to forage entirely on their own. The population dynamics of Canada geese are strongly influenced by adult survival rates, and the species' maximum lifespan in the wild of 42 years [am = 42 years] means that a single breeding pair can potentially contribute offspring to the population across many decades at a temperature of 41.1 °C [T = 41.1 °C]. This extended reproductive window, combined with the deferred first breeding at two years, ensures that only experienced breeders are responsible for the majority of recruitment into the population.
